paras: In 2022, an image made with the help of an artificial intelligence program won first prize in the digital art category of a state fair competition in Colorado. The artist had typed a series of prompts, generated hundreds of images, selected one and refined it. Several other entrants were furious, and the argument that followed spread far beyond the fairground. Was the winner an artist, a skilled user of software, or something the old vocabulary had no word for? Newspapers took sides, online forums filled with angry comments, and the artist himself insisted that he had broken no rules.

The question is not as new as it seems. When photography appeared in the nineteenth century, a number of critics insisted that a machine could not produce art, because the camera, not the person, did the work of representation. Some predicted that painting would soon be obsolete. Neither prediction survived. Photography became an art form of its own, and painting, freed from the obligation to record appearances, moved in directions it might never otherwise have taken. Is it not possible that something similar is happening again?

Possibly, but the comparison is not without its problems. A photographer chooses where to stand, when to press the shutter and what to leave outside the frame. A generative image program also involves choices, yet many of the decisions that shape the final image have been made in advance by a system trained on an enormous dataset of existing pictures, many of them created by artists who were never asked and are not credited. The objection that such images are derivative is therefore not unreasonable. The deeper difficulty, however, may be less about originality than about authorship: whose work, exactly, is inside the image?

A very different episode suggests that the art world has always been less interested in authorship alone than in stories about it. In 2018, moments after a framed canvas by the anonymous street artist Banksy sold at a London auction for more than a million pounds, a shredder hidden inside the frame began to cut the picture into strips. It stopped halfway. The artist later presented the half-destroyed work under a new title, and when it was sold again three years later, it fetched many times the original price. An iconoclastic gesture against the market had become, almost immediately, one of the market's most valuable commodities.

What connects a prize-winning AI image and a half-shredded canvas? Both remind us that the value of a work of art has never depended solely on the hand that made it. It depends on intention, on context, on the story told about the object and on the audience willing to believe that story. Connoisseurship once rested on the trained eye's ability to recognize an individual hand. It is hardly surprising that a technology which blurs the hand should leave so many people ambivalent.

None of this settles whether a machine can make art. It suggests, instead, that the question may be less useful than it looks. A more productive one might be what a particular work, however it was made, makes its viewers notice, and who is given credit for that act of attention. Those are questions that art historians, curators and, increasingly, lawyers will be asking for many years, and they are not questions a machine can answer on our behalf.

gist.prompt: Which statement best describes the writer's position?
choices: AI images are clearly not art, because machines have no intention.
The question of whether machines make art may matter less than questions of authorship, context and credit.
AI will make painting obsolete, just as photography did.

items: According to the writer, photography made painting obsolete.
'Some predicted that painting would soon be obsolete. Neither prediction survived.'
The writer considers the objection that AI images are derivative to be reasonable.
'The objection that such images are derivative is therefore not unreasonable.' Not unreasonable means reasonable.
The writer believes the comparison between cameras and AI programs is perfect.
'The comparison is not without its problems.' That means it has problems.
The half-shredded Banksy became far more valuable than before.
When sold again three years later, 'it fetched many times the original price'.
The writer finds it surprising that many people feel ambivalent about AI.
'It is hardly surprising' means it is not surprising at all.

parts: The auction had almost ended when the painting came up.
Bidding was quick, and within minutes the price passed a million pounds.
The auctioneer brought down the hammer.
Seconds later, an alarm sounded from inside the frame.
The canvas began to slide downward, emerging below the frame in thin strips.

tips: Deny the opposite, and sound more measured.
The auction was hardly an ordinary evening.
Hardly lowers the volume and raises the irony.

listenings.text: I have covered auctions for years, and most of them are, frankly, not very exciting. People raise paddles, a number goes up, someone says sold. That October evening in London was different. The painting was one of the last lots of the night, and the bidding went well past a million pounds. The auctioneer brought down the hammer, and then, a second or two later, an alarm started sounding from somewhere near the painting. Everyone turned. The canvas began sliding down through the bottom of its frame, and it came out underneath in long, thin strips. People gasped. A few laughed. Staff members rushed over. And then, about halfway through, it simply stopped, so the top of the picture was still there and the bottom hung in ribbons. Within a few days the artist had given the half-shredded work a new title, and when it came back to auction three years later, it sold for many times the original price. As protests against the art market go, it was not a complete success.

People often ask me whether the machine is the real artist in my studio, so let me describe what actually happens. I write code that trains a model on material I have chosen, often my own drawings, and then I ask it to suggest variations. Think of it as a very fast, very strange assistant. It shows me possibilities I would never have imagined, and most of them are terrible. I still decide what to keep, what to change and what to throw away, and that deciding is where I think the work lives. Now, I want to be honest about what worries me. Some of the popular image tools were trained on the work of millions of artists who were never asked and are not credited, and I do not think that problem is going away by itself. As for whether what I make is art, the question is not uninteresting, but I have stopped arguing about it. I would rather ask what the work makes people notice.
